title: Evaluating models honestly
summary: Confusion matrices, precision, recall and F1, the accuracy paradox and remedies for imbalanced classes, ROC and PR curves, cross-validation and hyperparameter tuning without leakage, and metrics for regression and segmentation including IoU.
syllabus: IOAI 1D1 Model Evaluation Metrics (Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1)
IOAI 1D5 Confusion Matrix and ROC Curves
IoU and mean IoU, R², MAE/RMSE, macro vs micro averaging
Class imbalance: class weights, resampling, SMOTE, cost-based thresholds

lessons.title: Confusion matrix, precision, recall and F1
lessons.summary: Counting the four kinds of right and wrong, the metrics built from them, and choosing the metric that matches the cost of errors.
objectives: You can fill a confusion matrix from predictions and a threshold
You can compute accuracy, precision, recall and F1 from counts
You can choose precision or recall for a given application

concepts.name: The threshold decides the confusion matrix
concepts.explain: A classifier outputs scores, and a threshold turns them into yes/no. Each prediction is a true positive, false positive, true negative or false negative. Raising the threshold makes the model pickier: fewer false positives (higher precision) but more false negatives (lower recall).
concepts.analogy: An airport scanner set to beep at the slightest metal catches every knife but annoys everyone wearing a belt.

visual.shows: Overlapping score histograms for the two classes with a draggable threshold, the 2×2 confusion matrix with counts, and bars for accuracy, precision, recall and F1.
visual.interaction: Drag the threshold; slide class separation and class imbalance; watch accuracy stay high while recall collapses on imbalanced data.
visual.aha: Precision and recall trade off through the threshold, and accuracy can hide a useless model.

concepts.name: F1: the harmonic mean
concepts.explain: F1 = 2PR / (P + R), the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It is high only when both are high, so a model with P = 1.0 and R = 0.1 has F1 of about 0.18, not 0.55.
concepts.analogy: Like a relay team that is only as fast as its two legs combined, punished heavily by one slow runner.

visual.shows: A plot comparing arithmetic and harmonic means as precision and recall vary.
visual.interaction: Drag precision and recall sliders; compare the two means.
visual.aha: The harmonic mean is dragged down by the weaker of the two.

concepts.name: Which error costs more?
concepts.explain: For cancer screening, missing a sick patient (false negative) is worst, so recall matters most. For a spam filter, losing a real email (false positive) is worse, so precision matters. F1 = 2PR/(P + R), the harmonic mean, is high only when both are high.
concepts.analogy: A lifeguard should overreact (high recall); a court should avoid convicting the innocent (high precision).

visual.shows: Scenario cards (screening, spam, fraud, face unlock) with an adjustable cost per FP and FN, and the threshold that minimises total cost.
visual.interaction: Pick a scenario and adjust costs; compare the cost-optimal threshold with the F1-optimal one.
visual.aha: The 'best' metric depends on the real-world cost of each kind of mistake.

checkpoint_focus: Screening favours recall; spam favours precision

lessons.title: Imbalanced classes
lessons.summary: Why accuracy lies when positives are rare, and the standard remedies.
objectives: You can explain the accuracy paradox
You can compare class weights, oversampling, SMOTE and undersampling
You can choose metrics for fraud and medical scenarios

concepts.name: The accuracy paradox
concepts.explain: With 1% positives, a model that always says 'negative' gets 99% accuracy and catches nothing. Accuracy is misleading for imbalanced data; use precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC or per-class metrics.
concepts.analogy: Like a security guard who never stops anyone being right 99.9% of the time while missing every thief.

visual.shows: A population grid with a slider for prevalence and the metrics of the 'always negative' model.
visual.interaction: Slide prevalence from 50% to 0.1%; accuracy climbs while recall stays at 0.
visual.aha: High accuracy can hide a useless model.

concepts.name: Remedies for imbalance
concepts.explain: Class weights scale the loss so rare-class errors cost more (e.g. weight 49 for a 2% class), keeping all data. Random oversampling duplicates minority samples; SMOTE creates synthetic ones by interpolating between neighbours; undersampling discards majority samples. Class weights are usually the practical first choice.
concepts.analogy: Like a teacher giving extra marks weight to the rare tough questions rather than photocopying them many times.

visual.shows: Tabs for each remedy showing the training set before and after, with pros and cons.
visual.interaction: Switch tabs; for SMOTE drag the interpolation slider to see synthetic points appear between neighbours.
visual.aha: Each remedy changes either the data or the loss; class weights change only the loss.

concepts.name: Choosing the metric by cost
concepts.explain: Match the metric to the cost of mistakes. Missed fraud costs money (prioritise recall), but too many false alarms swamp investigators (watch precision). Usually report F1 or PR-AUC plus the operating point you choose.
concepts.analogy: Like setting a smoke alarm: too sensitive and it rings when you cook, too lax and it misses a real fire.

visual.shows: A confusion matrix with adjustable costs for FP and FN and the threshold that minimises total cost.
visual.interaction: Change the costs; the optimal threshold and metrics move.
visual.aha: The right threshold depends on what errors cost.

checkpoint_focus: Class weights vs over/undersampling vs SMOTE

lessons.title: ROC and precision-recall curves
lessons.summary: Seeing performance across all thresholds at once, AUC, and why PR curves are better for rare positives.
objectives: You can plot TPR against FPR for several thresholds
You can interpret AUC (0.5 random, 1 perfect)
You can explain when to prefer a PR curve

concepts.name: Tracing the ROC curve
concepts.explain: As the threshold sweeps from high to low, the true positive rate and false positive rate both rise from 0 to 1; plotting one against the other gives the ROC curve. The area under it (AUC) is the probability that a random positive gets a higher score than a random negative: 0.5 is guessing and 1.0 is perfect.
concepts.analogy: Turning up the sensitivity of a metal detector step by step and recording how many coins versus bottle caps it beeps at.

visual.shows: Score histograms with a threshold line linked to a moving point on the ROC curve, with AUC shaded.
visual.interaction: Drag the threshold to move along the curve; slide class separation to see the curve bulge or flatten to the diagonal.
visual.aha: Every point on the ROC curve is one threshold; AUC summarises ranking quality independent of the threshold.

concepts.name: PR curves for rare positives
concepts.explain: When positives are rare, a small FPR can still mean many false positives compared with the few true positives, so the ROC curve looks great while precision is poor. The precision-recall curve exposes this because precision depends directly on the number of false positives.
concepts.analogy: A 1% false alarm rate sounds tiny until you screen a million transactions and get 10,000 false alarms for 100 real frauds.

visual.shows: ROC and PR curves for the same classifier side by side, with the positive-class rate adjustable.
visual.interaction: Slide the positive rate from 50% down to 0.5%; the ROC curve stays the same while the PR curve sinks.
visual.aha: For rare events, judge models by precision and recall, not by ROC AUC alone.

lessons.title: Cross-validation
lessons.summary: Why one validation split is not enough, k-fold cross-validation reported as mean ± standard deviation, stratified and grouped folds, and when the extra training is worth it.
objectives: You can run k-fold cross-validation, by hand and in code, and report the mean ± standard deviation of the fold scores
You can explain why classification needs stratified folds and why grouped or time-ordered rows need special folds
You can decide when cross-validation is worth its cost over a single split, and explain that the final model is retrained on all the training data

concepts.name: k-fold rotation
concepts.explain: Split the data into k folds; train on k − 1 folds and validate on the remaining one, rotating so every fold is the validation fold once. Average the k scores and report their spread. It uses data efficiently and gives a more stable estimate than one split, at k times the cost.
concepts.analogy: A class rotating the role of 'examiner' so everyone gets tested and everyone's marks count.

visual.shows: A data bar divided into k coloured folds with the validation fold moving along each round, and a dot plot of the k scores with mean and standard deviation.
visual.interaction: Slide k from 2 to 10; play the rotation; toggle stratification.
visual.aha: Cross-validation turns one noisy score into an average with error bars.

checkpoint_focus: CV scores a recipe; retrain on all the training data

lessons.title: Hyperparameter tuning without fooling yourself
lessons.summary: Grid and random search, keeping every fitted step inside the folds, and why tuning on the test set inflates the score, with nested cross-validation as the honest alternative.
objectives: You can compare grid search and random search for the same budget and count the models a search trains
You can explain why feature selection and every other fitted step must happen inside each fold, using a Pipeline
You can explain why the best of many test scores is biased upwards, and how nested cross-validation gives an honest estimate

concepts.name: Grid versus random search
concepts.explain: Grid search tries every combination on a fixed grid; random search samples combinations at random. When only one or two hyperparameters really matter, random search tries many more distinct values of them for the same budget.
concepts.analogy: Testing laksa recipes: a grid repeats the same 3 chilli levels many times, while random tries 9 different chilli levels.

visual.shows: A 2D hyperparameter space where only the x-axis matters (shown by a performance curve along the edge), with 9 grid points versus 9 random points and the best found by each.
visual.interaction: Change the budget; reshuffle the random points; change which axis matters.
visual.aha: Random search explores important hyperparameters more efficiently than a grid.

concepts.name: Keep selection inside the folds
concepts.explain: If you select features or fit a scaler using all the data and then cross-validate, the validation folds have already influenced training, so the CV score is optimistic. Putting preprocessing and selection in a Pipeline refits them on each training fold only.
concepts.analogy: Choosing which topics to revise after seeing the exam paper, then claiming your mock score predicts the real exam.

visual.shows: Two workflows on pure-noise data with many features: 'select then CV' reports well above chance, 'CV with selection inside' reports chance level.
visual.interaction: Slide the number of features and run both; the inflated score grows with more features.
visual.aha: With leakage, even random noise can look predictive.

concepts.name: Adaptive overfitting to the test set
concepts.explain: If you evaluate on the test set, tweak, and evaluate again many times, you are effectively tuning on the test set and the best score is biased upwards. Use a validation set (or CV) for tuning and touch the test set once.
concepts.analogy: Like retaking the same practice paper 50 times: your score rises but your real exam result does not.

visual.shows: Two protocols from the 2026 Prelim (repeated test evaluation vs train/val/test) with their reported and true scores.
visual.interaction: Increase the number of tuning iterations; the reported score in protocol A drifts above the true score.
visual.aha: Selection on a dataset spends its honesty.

checkpoint_focus: Counting the fits of a grid search
Nested CV for an honest estimate
Touch the test set once; tune on validation or CV

lessons.title: Regression metrics, IoU and averaging
lessons.summary: MAE, MSE, RMSE and R² for numbers; IoU (the Jaccard index) for boxes; macro versus micro averaging.
objectives: You can compute MAE, RMSE and R² for a small set
You can compute IoU for two boxes
You can tell macro from micro averaging

concepts.name: R² compares with predicting the mean
concepts.explain: R² = 1 − (sum of squared residuals)/(sum of squared deviations from the mean). It is 1 for perfect predictions, 0 for a model no better than always predicting the mean, and can be negative for worse models. RMSE is in the target's units, which makes it easier to explain.
concepts.analogy: Comparing your exam predictions with someone who just guesses the class average every time.

visual.shows: A scatter with the model line and the horizontal mean line; residual squares for both are drawn and their totals give R².
visual.interaction: Drag the model line; make it worse than the mean to see R² go negative.
visual.aha: R² measures improvement over the dumbest sensible baseline.

concepts.name: Intersection over union
concepts.explain: IoU = area of overlap / area of union, from 0 (no overlap) to 1 (perfect match); for sets it is called the Jaccard index. For two boxes, intersect their x-ranges and y-ranges to get the overlap rectangle (zero if either range is empty), then union = area A + area B − overlap. Detectors use box IoU to match predictions to ground truth and to suppress duplicate boxes. Per-pixel IoU for segmentation masks, and mean IoU over classes, come in the vision module.
concepts.analogy: Two people highlight the same paragraph: IoU is the shared highlighted part over everything highlighted by either.

visual.shows: Two draggable, resizable boxes with the intersection and union shaded and the areas computed step by step (overlap width × height, then union = A + B − overlap).
visual.interaction: Drag and resize the boxes; type coordinates to check a hand calculation; slide an IoU threshold to label the match a hit or a miss.
visual.aha: IoU punishes both missed and extra area, and box IoU is a few subtractions and one division.

concepts.name: Macro versus micro averaging
concepts.explain: Macro-averaging computes the metric per class and averages them equally, so rare classes count as much as common ones. Micro-averaging pools all predictions first, so common classes dominate. With imbalanced classes, macro-F1 reveals poor rare-class performance that micro-F1 hides.
concepts.analogy: Averaging each CCA's satisfaction score equally versus surveying every student in one big pool.

visual.shows: Per-class F1 bars for 3 classes with their sizes, plus the macro and micro averages.
visual.interaction: Change class sizes and per-class performance; watch the two averages diverge.
visual.aha: The averaging choice decides whether rare classes matter.

checkpoint_focus: Box IoU: union = A + B − overlap
